mappings.note: Mechanism of rusting plus the two necessary conditions - the 'explains corrosion' half of LO-7, with no prevention method asked for.
The prevention half of the same outcome: painting, greasing, galvanising. Paired with the rusting-mechanism item, the two split LO-7 cleanly between cause and cure.

Three unrelated sub-parts, one per code: surfaces dulling is corrosion (LO-7), aluminium by electrolysis of the molten ore is extraction (LO-6), and gold occurring native is a reactivity judgement (LO-2). Citing fewer codes would drop a whole sub-part.
Parts (a) and (b) are ionic bond formation and the resulting melting point, which only the competency covers; part (c) names the electrodes in electrolytic refining, which is LO-6.
Defines refining and describes the electrolytic cell - the purification stage that closes LO-6's extraction sequence.

All three parts are about the ionic compound - its formation by electron transfer, its hardness and its conduction only when molten. No outcome under C 1.1 reaches ionic compounds, so the competency carries the whole item.
Three candidate displacement equations to be accepted or rejected with reasons - LO-2's predictive clause applied three times, including one deliberate non-reaction.
Part (a) is the rationale for roasting and calcination before reduction (LO-6); part (b) justifies displacement reduction by ranking the reducing metal above the metal freed (LO-2).

Three sub-parts under three different codes: ionic melting points (competency, no outcome exists), why carbon cannot reduce highly reactive metals' oxides (LO-6), and the green patina on copper (LO-7).
Parts (a) soluble basic oxides and (c) softness of alkali metals are LO-1 properties; part (b), the protective oxide layer that makes the metal passive, is corrosion resistance under LO-7.
Gangue and the basis on which it is separated - the concentration stage that precedes reduction in LO-6's sequence.

Parts (a) and (b) classify elements from allotrope properties and oxide acidity (LO-1); part (c) is alloy-composition recall for bronze, which only LO-7 reaches, and weakly - see the reported alloy gap.

A passage-based item built entirely on the low/medium/high reactivity bands and their extraction routes, including why carbon cannot reduce alumina. This is LO-6's own wording expanded, so no second code is needed.
Full inventory of non-metal physical properties - the non-metal half of LO-1's classification criteria.
Collects the exceptions (mercury, gallium, caesium, iodine, graphite) that complicate classification by property. LO-1 is the outcome those exceptions qualify.

The body of the item is metals reacting with oxygen, water and dilute acids, with equations - LO-1 class properties. The opening 'in what forms are metals found' is a one-line lead-in answered as free or combined, with no ore treatment, so LO-6 is not cited.

Five reasons spanning all three: malleability and the nitric-acid exception are LO-1, jewellery metals' inertness and copper below hydrogen are LO-2, stainless steel not rusting is LO-7. DEFECT: sub-part (i) asks about gold and platinum but the key answers 'gold and silver', and sub-part (v)'s answer is typed 'Sinc'.
Copper from its sulphide ore plus electrolytic refining - two consecutive stages of LO-6, both asked in one item.

Parts (i) and (ii) identify sodium from its storage, ignition and basic oxide, with equations (LO-1); part (iii) then asks for its extraction from the molten chloride (LO-6). The item deliberately joins property to extraction route.
Five equations covering calcination, roasting, carbon reduction, sulphide self-reduction and thermite - every one an extraction stage under LO-6.

LO-6 leads because the demand is the extraction equations and the refining diagram; LO-1 is cited because the metal must first be identified from a physical property, its conductivity and use in wiring.
Naming the two most reactive metals is a series judgement (LO-2); drawing the electron transfer to a halogen and stating the compound's properties is bond formation, which only the competency covers.

Part (i) asks the student to DESIGN the three-test-tube activity that isolates air and moisture as the conditions for rusting - genuine investigation design, but C 8.2-LO-2 is worded only for comparing two METALS, so the competency C 8.2 had to be used instead. LO-7 carries the rusting and painting content.
Parts (a) mineral versus ore and (c) roasting are LO-6; parts (b) galvanisation and (d) amalgam fall under LO-7, which names galvanisation and alloying. Four sub-parts, two outcomes.

WEAK FIT. Definition of an alloy, how alloys are made, and the constituents and uses of three of them. Only 'alloying' in LO-7 connects, and that outcome frames alloying as corrosion prevention, which this item never mentions.
